transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-05
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Dana Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Luca Romano (Redwood SE), Ethan Park (StreamWorks CTO), Maya Lopez (Platform Eng), Jordan Kim (SRE), Taylor Nguyen (PM)
Shared: demo deck (link), benchmark spreadsheet (link), security packet (link)

00:00 Dana (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm dana from redwood inference, excited to walk through edge cases you flagged — long context, very high tps, and streaming backpressure/timeouts.
00:22 Ethan (StreamWorks CTO): thanks dana, yeah we have a bunch of customers running multi-document recall and long chat sessions, some sessions hit 80k tokens. our current infra starts to thrash once we hit sustained 2k tps for embeddings and ~300 rps for text gen.
00:45 Priya (Redwood SE): got it. quick question — when you say 80k tokens, is that full document plus history or mostly embeddings context?
00:58 Maya (Platform Eng): it's a mix. some use-cases are dense context windows where we append 50-100 attachments, others are conversation logs. we also do semantic search where we send large context payloads in the prompt.
01:20 Luca (Redwood SE): ok so two main axes: long-context sequence length affecting memory/kv-cache pressure, and high TPS affecting batching/backpressure behavior on streaming endpoints. we'll demo both and show mitigations.
01:38 Jordan (SRE): also want to call out timeouts — our frontend has 30s request timeouts; when streaming stalls we start dropping requests and the retries create spikes.
01:52 Dana: perfect, that's what we'll replicate. quick agenda: show console config, API examples (batching, streaming), optimize recommendations (quantization + caching), then a short benchmark story and next steps.

02:10 Priya: starting with console — here's the model route config (screen share). you can pin model versions, set batching window (we recommend 10-50ms for low latency workloads), and tune autoscale for Dedicated. note: Dedicated gives you predictable throughput so you don't get cross-tenant noisy neighbor spikes.
02:38 Maya: small question on dedicated — can we reserve burst above commit? like sudden spikes of 3x for a minute?
02:49 Dana: yes — burst capacity is configurable. you can set a burst budget that consumes spare pool or falls back to hosted variants; we can show pricing implications.
03:05 Priya: now API: for streaming we support chunked SSE and websocket. streaming preserves ordering and allows the client to consume partial tokens. important for backpressure: if the client stops reading, the runtime detects slow consumers and will apply per-connection buffers and backpressure policies — you can choose drop-latest, block, or fallback to non-streaming with a shorter response.
03:40 Ethan: Sounds good. what happens when KV cache grows because of long context across many concurrent requests?
03:50 Luca: good point. our runtime shards KV per-worker and uses LRU eviction plus prefix-level caching. for extremely long context we suggest prefix-KV caching (cache the expensive static prefix) and then stream only the dynamic tail. also recommend model quantization profiles for memory efficiency.
04:12 Maya: any numbers? like for 80k tokens what's memory footprint and latency impact?
04:20 Priya: rough numbers: an 80k context with a 4k model window requires out-of-core strategies, but if you split the prompt into cached prefix + short active window you can cut active kv memory by 60-80%. for latency: cold paths can be >5s per request for generation; with prefix caching and optimized kernels that goes down to sub-second for token start and streaming fills afterwards. these are approximate — the benchmark will give precise numbers.

05:00 Dana: demo time — we'll trigger three scenarios: A) long-context single request (80k tokens) on hosted, B) high TPS burst test (~2k tps) on Dedicated, C) streaming with introduced slow-client backpressure to replicate front-end 30s timeouts.
05:20 Priya: starting scenario A — sending a single long-context request (showing curl).
05:35 console (automated voice): request sent.
05:40 Priya: transcript — you might hear some latency; the runtime is fetching prefix from KV cache then compiling kernels for the long sequence. transcription note: the automated capture sometimes renders 'KV cash' or 'kv-cash' in the transcript.
06:00 Ethan: (background) okay seeing the request land.
06:20 Priya: result — partial stream begins at ~0.9s then steadies. we see a spike in memory usage on the worker since it's handling large attention windows. on hosted this triggered a model compile step, which is why cold-start was higher.
06:45 Jordan: is there a per-request timeout in the runtime? we saw the frontend time out at 30s — does Redwood keep working after client disconnect?
06:55 Luca: by default we continue the inference for a short grace period (10s) to finish in-flight generation unless you configure 'abort on disconnect'. we log aborted requests and can forward partial artifact to storage. this avoids wasted compute in many cases.

07:20 Priya: moving to scenario B — high TPS. we're using the benchmark harness (link). sending a synthetic mix: 70% embeddings small payloads, 20% short text gen, 10% long context retrieval. target sustained 2k tps.
07:40 automated: load started — generating RPS curve.
07:48 Dana: watch latency percentiles in the console — p50, p95, p99. we also show token-level CPU/GPU utilization.
08:05 Maya: we're seeing p99 spike to 1.2s then climb to 3s on the hosted run.
08:12 Priya: expected — hosted operates with multi-tenant packing; Dedicated would mask this with reserved GPUs. also our smart routing can split requests by policy — route high-priority traffic to Dedicated and low-priority to hosted variants.
08:30 Ethan: can we do autoscale fast enough? spikes are often short (30-90s).
08:38 Luca: autoscale uses predictive scaling + burst budget; Dedicated can pre-warm nodes based on traffic hooks and we offer instant burst via a reserved spare pool. you can also set a warm-up policy to keep a small buffer of idle capacity during business hours.

09:00 Priya: now scenario C — streaming backpressure case: we'll simulate a slow client that reads slowly and a 30s frontend timeout.
09:15 automated: introducing 30s read blockade on 25% of streams.
09:22 Jordan: that's our real problem — once clients timeout and retry, the retry fanout amplifies load.
09:30 Priya: right. mitigation options: 1) at client: implement exponential backoff + jitter and detect idempotency keys; 2) at route level: enable per-connection rate limits and drop policies (e.g., drop-latest) or short-circuit streaming to a non-streaming summary; 3) at infra: tune streaming buffers and enable proxy-level backpressure propagation (so upstream slows down request acceptance).
09:58 Ethan: what's the default drop policy?
10:03 Priya: default is 'block then fallback' for hosted; for Dedicated you can pick 'drop-latest' to preserve overall throughput. we also surface metrics for slow consumer counts to alert on growing backpressure.

10:30 Dana: quick interlude — security: you asked about SOC 2, SSO, KMS. we have SOC 2 Type II, SAML/Okta SSO, and KMS/HSM integrations. for Private deployments we can run your control plane in your VPC and integrate with customer KMS for per-tenant key control.
10:50 Maya: good — can we get the security packet?
10:54 Dana: yes sending after call.

11:10 Priya: back to tuning: Optimize recommendations — quantization profiles (4-bit/8-bit depending on model family), kernel selection, and intelligent batching. for high tps embedding workloads, batch windows of 20-40ms with dynamic batching gives best throughput without hurting p95 too much.
11:35 Luca: also consider caching embedding outputs for repeated queries — we support an LRU semantic cache at the route level. that can reduce upstream calls by 30-70% depending on duplication.

12:00 Maya: curious about model fallback — if the primary model runs out of capacity, what's the behavior?
12:08 Dana: automatic fallback: you can define a policy to route to a cheaper quantized variant, or to a smaller model. there's also automatic downgrade for non-critical paths. you can set preservation rules for high-SLA customers.

12:30 Priya: demo of failure/fallback — simulating out-of-capacity on Dedicated triggers routing to hosted fallback and notifies via console. we also show logs and trace-ID mapping back to the request.
12:55 Jordan: nice. how granular are the cost/latency breakdowns? we need per-token, per-route, and per-customer spend.
13:05 Dana: console gives token-level cost estimates, grouping by model, route, and token type (context vs generated). we also provide tooling to export to billing systems.

13:30 Priya: now live bench results summary (we ran a parallel benchmark earlier): hosted at 2k tps showed p95 = 1.1s for embeddings, but text gen p95 spiked when long-context requests were in flight; Dedicated baseline reduced variance and brought p99 down by ~40% in sustained runs. streaming slow-client scenarios improved by enabling backpressure propagation and setting drop-latest for non-critical streams.

14:05 Ethan: are there SDK hooks for detecting slow clients so we can fail fast?
14:12 Luca: yes — our SDK exposes events for stream lag and provides client-side buffering helpers plus sample code for backpressure-aware reads. we'll drop those in the repo.

14:30 Maya: a practical ask — can Redwood handle our mixed workload: 60% embeddings (small), 30% short gen (<=512 tokens), 10% long retrieval (>=20k tokens) and a spike pattern of 2-3x for 60-90s daily?
14:48 Dana: yes — recommended architecture: Dedicated for critical short-gen and embeddings with autoscale + burst, hosted fallback for overflow, prefix-KV caching for long retrieval, and Optimize recommendations (batching + quantization) to reduce unit costs. we'll size Dedicated nodes based on your p90 throughput and keep burst budget for daily spikes.
15:10 Priya: follow-up on measurement — we'll need sample traces to tune kernels and batching heuristics. the plan: StreamWorks provides traces, we run a 48h benchmark with your traffic shape, and then deliver a sizing + cost estimate.
15:28 Ethan: timeline looks good.

15:40 Dana: recap of next steps — send pricing, security packet, and benchmark plan. action owners: priya to run benchmarks, dana to handle pricing, ethan to send traces. any final Qs?
15:55 Taylor (PM): curious about SLAs — can we get 99.9 for Dedicated?
16:05 Dana: yes we offer SLA-backed availability for Dedicated; latency SLOs depend on workload but we can carve an SLA for critical routes in the contract.
16:18 Maya: one more — if we go Private deployment later, how different is the console/observability?
16:26 Luca: same console UX; your control plane is in your VPC and we stream telemetry back to your chosen storage. audit logs and RBAC integrate with your IdP. small differences in network topology documented in the private deployment guide.

16:45 Priya: ok i will share the benchmark scripts and a short README. internal note: sometimes the auto transcription writes 'Redwood Dedicates' or 'k v cache' — ignore that in the transcript.
17:00 Ethan: thanks everyone this was helpful.
17:10 Dana: thanks all — we'll follow up by end of week.

17:25 automated: meeting ended.
